messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 37
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Refugee Aid Worker
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Authority Presence: Police, Others Cycling: People cycling, Crowding/Overstimulation: Crowded spaces
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Positive Events: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
  Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm, Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
  Negative Appraisals: Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

Vignette:
Linh Nguyen is a 37-year-old married Vietnamese American woman who works as a refugee aid worker, and when she first spoke about the event, she did so in short, interrupted stretches, as if staying with it for more than a few seconds would pull her back into it. Several months ago, she was leaving a community outreach meeting in a downtown corridor crowded with food vendors, cyclists cutting between pedestrians, and uniformed officers managing traffic around a demonstration nearby. Linh remembered the press of bodies first, then the sharp sense of being hemmed in. A bicycle came too close, someone shouted, and in the confusion she was knocked off balance just as police surged toward the crowd. She described seeing uniforms and raised voices at close range, feeling trapped in the noise and movement, and then being handled with force by officers who seemed to take her attempts to explain herself as resistance. What stayed with her was not only the physical fear but the sense of helpless exposure: people were everywhere, no one intervened, and afterward nothing about it felt acknowledged or put right. When she recalls it now, she is overcome by grief as much as fear, grieving the person she feels she was before that day and the ease with which she once moved through the city and through her work.

In the weeks that followed, Linh found that ordinary parts of her day had become charged. Police cars parked outside municipal buildings where she accompanied clients made her body tense before she had even consciously registered why. If an officer entered a lobby where she was waiting with a family, she would immediately begin scanning for exits and trying to position herself away from them. People cycling past her on the sidewalk produced a jolt that felt out of proportion to the moment but entirely convincing to her; the quick approach, the narrow gap, the unpredictability all landed in her body as danger. Crowded spaces became especially difficult. Her job often required her to help newly arrived families navigate busy offices, transit stations, and waiting rooms, yet in those settings she felt flooded by noise and movement, and she would hurry interactions along or ask colleagues to take over. She did not tell most people why. She had come to believe that somebody else would not have gotten into that situation in the first place, that a more competent, more alert version of herself would have moved differently or spoken differently and avoided what happened.

Linh tried hard not to think about the incident. She kept herself busy, redirected her mind, and cut off conversations if they drifted toward protests, policing, or public safety. When memories broke through anyway, they did not come as distant recollections. She felt the same terror she had felt at the time, along with such a rush of emotion that she would have to stop whatever she was doing, sometimes shutting herself in a bathroom at work until she could get herself back under control. She said the worst part was how quickly the memory tipped into grief. She would think, with a force that felt undeniable, that what happened to her was deeply unfair and that nothing had been done about it. The event sat in her mind as unresolved, almost intolerably so.

Over the following months her life narrowed in other ways. Linh began turning away from things that might have made her feel happy or hopeful. If her husband suggested dinner with friends, a day trip, or a celebration, she found reasons not to go. Hopefulness felt exposed and unsafe to her, as though letting herself enjoy something would only make the loss more obvious afterward. She became more irritable at home and at work, snapping at small delays and reacting sharply when colleagues interrupted her or clients arrived late. She was sleeping poorly, lying awake long after bedtime and waking through the night, already braced. At times she also sought out bursts of excitement that cut through the deadened vigilance she carried during the day. She began gambling online late at night, telling herself it distracted her and gave her something else to focus on. There were also moments when she noticed herself taking chances that did not feel like her—crossing streets carelessly, moving too fast through situations she would once have approached more steadily—followed by a detached sense that harm no longer felt as avoidable as it once had.

What troubles Linh nearly as much as the fear is the conviction that she no longer knows herself. She had always experienced herself as calm, purposeful, and grounded in difficult environments, someone other people could rely on. Now, in the very settings where she built her career—crowded government offices, shelters, public transit, city sidewalks—she feels brittle, watchful, and estranged from that earlier identity. She finally sought help after a recent workday when she froze outside a packed service center as two police officers stood near the entrance and a stream of cyclists passed in front of the building. She handed her clients off to a coworker and went home ashamed and shaken. By the time she came in, she was frightened that this was becoming her life: avoiding joy, avoiding parts of her work, sleeping badly, feeling angry and reckless, and being unable to remember the event without terror and grief. What she hopes for most is not to erase what happened, but to feel like herself again.
